A node is internal when it has at least one child. With height measured as the number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path, a height-7 tree has levels 0 to 7, and the maximum is reached by the perfect tree with 2^8 - 1 = 255 nodes. The 2^7 = 128 nodes at level 7 are all leaves, so every internal node lies on levels 0 to 6, giving 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + 64 = 2^7 - 1 = 127. That is both an upper bound and achievable, so 127 is the answer.

Why B is correct: 127 = 2^7 - 1 is exactly the number of nodes on levels 0 through 6, which is the set of internal nodes of a perfect height-7 binary tree.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: 128 = 2^7 counts the leaves sitting at level 7, not internal nodes.
- C: 64 = 2^6 counts only the nodes at level 6.
- D: 63 = 2^6 - 1 would be the internal count only if height were measured in levels instead of edges.

A single quicksort partition leaves the pivot sitting at its final sorted position: every element smaller than the pivot is on its left and every element larger is on its right. For 10, 8, 6, 9, 11, 14, 16, 15 a pivot of 11 is legal since 10, 8, 6, 9 are smaller and 14, 16, 15 are larger, and a pivot of 14 is equally legal since 10, 8, 6, 9, 11 are smaller and 16, 15 are larger. Both partitions can be produced, so the pivot cannot be pinned to one element.

Why C is correct: Both 11 and 14 satisfy the partition property for this sequence, so either one could have been the pivot of the first partition.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: it claims 14 could not be the pivot, but 10, 8, 6, 9, 11 are all below 14 and 16, 15 above it.
- B: it claims 11 could not be the pivot, but 10, 8, 6, 9 are below 11 and 14, 16, 15 above it.
- D: one partition produces exactly one pivot, so 11 and 14 cannot both be pivot elements.

Recursion trades memory for brevity: every active call frame consumes stack space, so a recursive version uses more memory, not less. What recursion buys you is expressiveness, because the definition of the problem naturally restates itself, which usually means less code and less bookkeeping than an explicit loop with a manual stack.

Why B is correct: Recursion lets the problem be written in terms of itself, so the solution is shorter and easier to implement than the iterative version.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: recursion consumes more memory, since each call frame is held on the stack.
- C: this is true of recursion but it is a disadvantage, not an advantage, so it cannot be the answer.
- D: 'All the options' cannot hold because A is false and C states the opposite of an advantage.

One bubble-sort pass sweeps from left to right comparing neighbours and swapping out-of-order pairs. On LA = {1, 2, 4, 3} the comparisons are 1 vs 2 (no swap), 2 vs 4 (no swap) and 4 vs 3 (swap), which yields {1, 2, 3, 4}. The array is therefore sorted after a single pass, and running the loop confirms one pass suffices.

Why C is correct: Only the 4 and 3 are out of order, and one left-to-right pass fixes that single inversion and leaves the whole array sorted.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: four passes are the worst case for four elements that are in reverse order, which this array is not.
- B: two passes would only be needed if an element other than 4 had been left out of place after the first pass.
- D: zero passes is impossible because 1, 2, 4, 3 is not already sorted.

For T(n) = 7T(n/3) + n^2 log n we have a = 7, b = 3, so n^(log_b a) = n^(log_3 7) and log_3 7 is about 1.771. The toll f(n) = n^2 log n is polynomially larger than n^1.771 (it carries an extra n^0.23 factor on top of a log factor), so Master Theorem case 3 applies and the toll dominates. Hence T(n) = Theta(n^2 log n).

Why A is correct: Since f(n) = n^2 log n polynomially dominates n^(log_3 7), case 3 of the Master Theorem gives Theta(n^2 log n).

The cheapest way to validate a BST is a single inorder traversal that checks that the visited keys are strictly increasing, which touches every node exactly once. Any correct test must at least read every node, since a single unread node could hold a key that violates the ordering, so Omega(n) is a lower bound and the traversal achieves it.

Why B is correct: One inorder traversal that verifies strict increase runs in O(n) time and every node must be inspected, so O(n) is the minimum.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: O(1) would mean deciding from a single node, but any node can hide a violation elsewhere in the tree.
- C: O(log n) is only achievable for balanced trees; a skewed BST still needs all n nodes visited.
- D: O(n log n) would be wasteful, since the inorder traversal alone suffices without any extra factor of log n.

For a circular array with an explicit count, the number of elements is count = (rear - front + maxsize) mod maxsize + 1. Substituting front = 0 and rear = maxsize - 1 gives count = maxsize, i.e. every slot is occupied and the queue is full. Taking maxsize = 4, which is what the option set presumes, count is 4.

Why C is correct: front = 0 with rear = maxsize - 1 fills every slot, so the count equals maxsize, which is 4 under the size implied by the options.

- A: 0 would mean the queue is empty, which is the front = rear = -1 case, not front = 0 with rear = maxsize - 1.
- B: 3 would correspond to front = 0 and rear = maxsize - 2.
- D: 2 would correspond to only two occupied slots.

Scheduling and resource allocation are both first-come-first-served problems: the process that has waited longest should get the CPU or the resource next. That is exactly the discipline a FIFO queue enforces, so queue is the data structure applied directly to both problems.

Why B is correct: Queue models the fair, arrival-order discipline used for process scheduling and resource allocation.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: stack is LIFO, which starves older requests and is not used for scheduling.
- C: tree offers no arrival-order fairness, so it is not applied directly to scheduling.
- D: linked list is only a storage mechanism and does not itself provide the FCFS discipline.

A stack can be simulated with two queues: push onto an 'in' queue, and to pop transfer every element of 'in' into an 'out' queue and then dequeue from 'out', which reverses the order. One queue alone also works but only if you are allowed to rotate it n times on every pop, which costs O(n) per operation rather than the O(1) amortised behaviour of the two-queue scheme.

Why D is correct: Two queues give constant-time pushes and amortised constant-time pops by reversing the in-queue into an out-queue on demand.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: a single queue only simulates a stack efficiently if each pop costs O(n) rotations, which defeats the purpose.
- B: three queues are not required; two suffice.
- C: four queues are unnecessary, since the standard construction uses exactly two.

Items (i) and (ii) are classic LIFO uses of a stack: reversing a string and tracking nested function calls both depend on the most recent item being served first. Items (iii) and (iv) need no stack at all, because sorting is done by comparison-based algorithms and simply walking an array from index 0 upward prints it in its original order. So (iii) and (iv) are the ones you would not use a stack for.

Why C is correct: Sorting the array and printing it in its existing order both need no stack, since neither relies on last-in-first-out access.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: reversing a name is done precisely by pushing every character and popping them back, so (i) is a genuine stack use.
- B: nested function calls are managed with a call stack, so (ii) is a genuine stack use.
- D: at least (i) and (ii) are valid stack applications, so 'none of the options' is not right.

Online multiplayer games must serve players according to status rather than arrival time, for example match quality, rank or session priority. A priority queue orders elements by a key rather than by insertion time, which is exactly what such matchmaking needs, whereas a simple, circular or single-ended queue can only serve players in arrival order.

Why C is correct: Priority queue selects the next player by priority key, which is what online game matchmaking requires.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: simple queue is strictly FIFO and cannot rank players by importance.
- B: circular queue only recycles slots of a fixed array and gives no priority ordering.
- D: single ended queue is just a restricted FIFO and offers no ordering by priority.

The decisive detail is that the last node points back to the first node, which makes the list circular. Because every node has only one link field, there is no backward pointer, so the list is singly rather than doubly linked. Together these give a singly circular linked list.

Why C is correct: One forward link per node makes it singly linked, and the last node pointing back to the first makes it circular.

- B: a doubly linked list would need a prev pointer in every node, which is not described.
- D: a doubly circular list would need both a next and a prev link in each node.

Evaluating the postfix expression x 12 + z 17 y + 42 * / + with a stack: x and 12 give (x + 12); 17 and y give (17 + y); that result times 42 gives ((17 + y) * 42); then z is divided by it; finally the two partial sums are added. The infix form is therefore x + 12 + z / ((17 + y) * 42), and the parentheses around (17 + y) * 42 are forced by the postfix grouping.

Why A is correct: The postfix groups 17 + y, multiplies it by 42, divides z by that product, then adds the x + 12 term, giving x + 12 + z / ((17 + y) * 42).

Why the others are wrong:
- B: x + 12 + z / 17 + y * 42 drops the parentheses that the postfix structure forces around (17 + y) and 42.
- C: x + 12 + z / (17 + y) * 42 applies * and / left to right instead of dividing z by the whole product.
- D: x + (12 + z) / (17 + y * 42) binds the wrong operands together and misplaces the final addition.

Big-O is closed under addition, so if T1(n) <= c1 F(n) and T2(n) <= c2 F(n) for large n, then T1(n) + T2(n) <= (c1 + c2) F(n), which is again O(F(n)). It is not closed under multiplication, since O(F) times O(F) is only O(F^2). Nor does being bounded by the same function make two functions equal or comparable in the big-O sense, because they may still differ wildly in growth rate.

Why A is correct: The sum of two O(F(n)) functions is O(F(n)), because the two constants add into a single constant.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: multiplying two O(F(n)) functions gives at best O(F(n)^2), not O(F(n)).
- C: two functions being bounded by the same F says nothing about either being O(1).
- D: T1 could be n^2 and T2 could be n while both are O(n^2), and n^2 is not O(n), so the implication fails.

A simple connected graph on v vertices has at least v - 1 edges, so B is always true, and at most v(v-1)/2 edges which is certainly at most v^2, so A is always true. The inequality v >= e/2, however, fails as soon as the graph is dense enough: for K6 we have v = 6 and e = 15, so e/2 = 7.5 which is greater than 6. The claim therefore does not hold in general.

Why C is correct: For K6, e = 15 and e/2 = 7.5 exceeds v = 6, so v >= e/2 is violated by a simple connected graph.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: e <= v^2 always holds because the true maximum v(v-1)/2 is smaller than v^2.
- B: e >= v - 1 always holds for any connected graph, by the definition of connectivity.
- D: 'All the options' cannot be the answer to a 'which is not correct' question while C is in fact incorrect.

With exactly two nodes in a circular doubly linked list, head and tail each point to the other node. So head->next = tail is true, head->prev = tail and therefore head->prev->next = tail->next = head, which is not tail, so B is false. The remaining two statements hold: tail->prev = head so tail->prev->next = head->next = tail, and tail->next = head so tail->next->prev = head->prev = tail.

Why B is correct: head->prev is tail and tail->next is head, so head->prev->next evaluates to head, not tail.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: head->next = tail is true because the two nodes are adjacent in both directions.
- C: tail->prev is head and head->next is tail, so the statement holds.
- D: tail->next is head and head->prev is tail, so the statement holds.

The next two Pop(&A) calls move 4 and then 8 to B, so B becomes 9, 7, 3, 5, 4, 8 with 8 on top. The four Pop(&B) calls then print 8, 4, 5, 3, 7, 9 in that order, which matches option B.

Why B is correct: Simulating the sequence prints 8 4 5 3 7 9, exactly the values in option B.

Why the others are wrong:

- C: 3 4 8 5 7 9 would require the elements of A to be pushed back onto A in the wrong order.

Starting empty: push 2 and push 3 leaves [2, 3]; pop leaves [2]; push 3 gives [2, 3]; pop gives [2]; pop empties it; push 2 gives [2]; pop empties it; the final pop then tries to remove an element from an empty stack. The stack never holds more than two elements so size 4 is never exceeded, and the failure is an underflow.

Why A is correct: The ninth operation is a Pop on an already empty stack, which raises stack underflow.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: overflow needs a push onto a full stack, and at most two elements are ever present in a size-4 stack.
- C: the final Pop cannot succeed because the stack is empty at that point.

f(n) = n^2 + 3n + 4 grows like n^2 while g(n) = n^3 grows strictly faster, so f(n) / g(n) = (n^2 + 3n + 4) / n^3 tends to 0. Since f(n) <= c * g(n) for a suitable constant c (in fact for all n >= 1), f(n) = O(g(n)). The reverse bound fails because g(n) / f(n) grows without limit.

Why A is correct: n^3 eventually dominates n^2 + 3n + 4, so f is bounded above by a constant multiple of g, which is exactly f(n) = O(g(n)).

Why the others are wrong:
- B: f(n) = Theta(g(n)) would require the ratio to tend to a positive constant, but it tends to 0.
- C: g(n) = O(f(n)) would require a constant upper bound on n^3 / (n^2 + 3n + 4), which is unbounded.
- D: g(n) = Theta(f(n)) is also false for the same reason, and Theta is a two-sided statement.

Pushing 4, 8, 12, 16 leaves 16 on top. The first two pops return 16 and 12, whose sum 28 is pushed back, giving the stack 4, 8, 28. The second pair of pops returns 28 and 8, whose sum 36 is pushed, leaving the stack 4, 36 with 36 on top. So the current top of the stack is 36.

Why C is correct: The two rounds of pop-pair-and-push-sum give 16 + 12 = 28 and then 28 + 8 = 36, and 36 ends up on top.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: 4 is left at the bottom of the stack, not on top.
- B: 16 was popped off in the very first pair of operations.
- D: 28 is the intermediate result after the first round, before the second round replaces it.

A complete graph connects every pair of distinct vertices, so it has one edge for each unordered pair. Counting those pairs gives n choose 2 = n(n - 1)/2, which for n = 4 gives 6 edges.

Why A is correct: The number of unordered vertex pairs in a complete graph on n vertices is n(n - 1)/2.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: n(n + 1)/2 is the count of pairs allowing self-pairs, which a simple graph does not have.
- C: 2n would be right only if every vertex had degree 2, as in a cycle.
- D: n/2 has no combinatorial meaning here and is far too small.

Every finite DAG has at least one vertex of in-degree 0, because following incoming edges backwards must eventually stop, so the minimum in-degree is 0. The maximum out-degree is at least 1, since a DAG with more than one vertex cannot have every vertex at out-degree 0, and for a single isolated vertex the two are 0 and 0 giving sum 0. For any DAG with an edge the sum is therefore strictly positive.

Why C is correct: In any non-trivial DAG the minimum in-degree is 0 and the maximum out-degree is at least 1, so their sum is greater than zero.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: the sum is not always zero, since a DAG such as a single edge 1 to 2 gives 0 + 1 = 1.
- B: the sum is fixed by the acyclic structure of the DAG, it does not vary arbitrarily with the graph.
- D: 'None of the options' is wrong because option C states the standard result.

Two facts separate graph traversal from tree traversal. First, a graph may contain cycles, so a traversal must carry a visited marker to avoid looping forever, which a tree never needs. Second, DFS on a general graph must keep explicit state and is normally written with a stack, whereas the standard tree traversals such as inorder are written as simple self-recursive routines. Both differences are real.

Why C is correct: Both listed properties hold, because graphs may contain cycles and DFS on a graph relies on an explicit stack while inorder traversal of a tree is naturally recursive.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: cycles are a genuine difference but not the only one stated in the question, so listing only this property is incomplete.
- B: the DFS versus recursive-inorder contrast is genuine but again only covers one of the two differences.
- D: 'None of the options' is wrong because the two properties above are both true.

A tree has a single well-defined root from which traversal descends, so no bookkeeping is needed to know where to begin or when to stop. A graph has no root, so the traversal must pick a start vertex, carry a visited set to survive cycles, and restart on each unvisited component. Of the three stated reasons, only the presence of a root is a true statement at all.

Why C is correct: A tree has a unique root that anchors traversal, whereas a graph has none, which forces visited tracking and multiple start points.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: trees are not binary in general, only binary trees have at most two children, so this is factually false.
- B: a tree is a well-defined structure, so 'tree is undefined' is not a reason for anything.
- D: 'All the options' cannot be right because option A is false.
answers.reviewReason: All three stated reasons are poor; the real cause is cycles and the absence of a root, and option A ('tree is binary') is factually wrong, so only C is defensible.

Binary search removes the comparison cost of finding the insert position, dropping it to O(log n) per insertion. It does not remove the shifting cost: on the worst-case input (reverse sorted) every one of the n insertions must shift O(n) elements to open the gap. Since the shifts dominate, the total worst case stays at O(n^2); only the constant factor improves.

Why C is correct: Even with an O(log n) binary search per element, the O(n) shifting per insertion still totals O(n^2) in the worst case.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: O(n log n) would require the shifting to cost O(1) per insertion, which no array implementation achieves.
- B: O(n) is impossible because reverse-sorted input forces n(n-1)/2 element moves.
- D: O(1) would mean insertion sort does no per-element work at all, which is absurd.

The loop must keep shifting elements right while there is something to the left of position j that is bigger than the value being inserted. That is exactly (j > 0) && (arr[j - 1] > value): j > 0 protects arr[j - 1] from going before the start of the array, and arr[j - 1] > value says the element at j - 1 belongs further right. Using || instead would keep the loop running after j reaches 0.

Why B is correct: The shift loop must continue while j is still inside the array and while the element to the left of j exceeds value, which is precisely (j > 0) && (arr[j-1] > value).

Why the others are wrong:
- A: using || makes the loop run even when j is 0 or when arr[j-1] is not greater, writing out of bounds.
- C: arr[j+1] looks to the right of the current position, but the loop shifts elements from the left.
- D: arr[j+1] < value compares the wrong element in the wrong direction and would never terminate correctly.

For a connected planar graph drawn on a plane, Euler's formula gives V - E + F = 2, where F counts all regions including the unbounded outer one. Substituting V = 6 and E = 7 gives F = 2 - 6 + 7 = 3. So the graph divides the plane into three regions, one of which is the outer face.

Why D is correct: Euler's formula gives F = 2 - V + E = 2 - 6 + 7 = 3 regions including the outer face.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: 11 would need V = 6, E = 2 by the same formula, which is impossible for a connected graph.
- B: 15 would need E = 19, far more than a planar graph on 6 vertices can have (at most 12).
- C: 1 region would mean no edge existed at all, but the graph has seven.

Inserting 7, 4, 6, 1, 2, 3, 8, 5 gives 7 at the root with 4 and 8 as children; 4 has children 1 and 6; 1 has right child 2; 2 has right child 3; 6 has left child 5. The longest root-to-leaf path is 7-4-1-2-3, which uses four edges, and a recursive height computation confirms the height is 4 edges (5 levels).

Why A is correct: The deepest path 7, 4, 1, 2, 3 spans four edges, so with height measured in edges the tree has height 4.

Why the others are wrong:

- C: 7 is the number of keys inserted, not the height.
- D: 2 is far too small, since the left subtree alone is three levels deep.

As written the question does not specify what kind of tree or what distinguishes the nodes, so no standard counting formula applies cleanly: the number of distinct binary tree shapes on 10 nodes is the Catalan number 16796, and the number of labelled trees is n^(n-2), neither of which appears here. Why B is correct: Under the intended doubling argument each additional node doubles the number of possibilities, so ten nodes give 2^10 = 1024.

Why the others are wrong:

- C: 1014 is not a power of two and matches no counting formula.
- D: 90 is far too small; even a balanced binary tree on 10 nodes admits many more shapes.

The standard construction uses two queues: pushes go into an 'in' queue and a pop reverses the in-queue into an 'out' queue by transferring every element and then dequeuing, which restores LIFO order. A single queue works only if each pop rotates the queue n times, costing O(n) per operation, so it is not efficient.

Why A is correct: Two queues are enough to simulate a stack with constant-time pushes and amortised constant-time pops.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: three queues are more than the two the standard construction needs.
- C: one queue only works with an O(n) rotation on every pop, which is not efficient.
- D: 'Atleast 3' contradicts the two-queue construction and also duplicates option B.

A full binary tree, in the standard sense that every node has either 0 or 2 children, always contains an odd number of nodes, so 8 and 14 are excluded. That leaves both 15 and 13, and both are achievable: 15 is a perfect tree of height 4, and 13 is 6 leaves plus 7 internal nodes, which can be realised as a complete full tree. If 'full' is instead taken to mean perfect, only 2^k - 1 node counts work and 15 is the unique answer.

Why B is correct: 15 = 2^4 - 1 is a perfect binary tree node count and 15 is odd, so it can certainly form a full binary tree.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: 8 is even, and a full binary tree always has an odd number of nodes.
- C: 13 is also odd and can form a full binary tree, so the question does not have a unique answer under the standard definition.
- D: 14 is even, so it cannot form a full binary tree.
answers.reviewReason: Both 13 and 15 satisfy the standard definition of a full binary tree (odd node count), so two options are defensible; 15 is chosen as the unique answer only if 'full' is read as 'perfect'.

An adjacency matrix stores one entry for every ordered pair of vertices, so it is a v by v array of booleans or weights. That is v^2 cells regardless of how sparse the graph is, giving O(n^2) memory, which is why the matrix is preferred for dense graphs and adjacency lists for sparse ones.

Why B is correct: The matrix has one cell per vertex pair, so it occupies n squared cells and O(n^2) memory.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: O(n) would be the size of an adjacency list, not of a matrix.
- C: O(n^3) would require three nested indices, which a matrix does not have.
- D: O(log n) is far too small for any representation that must record arbitrary pairs.

A polynomial in the general case is a sparse sequence of terms, and each term contributes two values, its coefficient and its exponent, which may be non-consecutive. A linked list of (coefficient, exponent) nodes stores exactly these pairs and handles gaps and varying degree naturally, whereas a plain array would waste most of its slots on missing powers.

Why B is correct: A linked list of coefficient/exponent pairs stores a sparse polynomial compactly.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: an array needs a slot for every exponent from 0 up to the degree and wastes most of them when terms are missing.
- C: a queue imposes a fixed insertion discipline that does not match polynomial storage.
- D: a stack imposes LIFO order, which does not match polynomial storage.

Converting infix to postfix requires knowing whether the operator currently being read is already applied to an expression, that is, whether it still has to wait for its right operand. That is precisely a stack discipline: operators are pushed when encountered and popped when a lower-precedence operator or the end of the expression arrives, and operands are emitted directly.

Why B is correct: A stack holds pending operators in precedence order, which is exactly what the infix to postfix conversion needs.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: a linked list gives no natural way to order pending operators by precedence.
- C: a queue is FIFO and cannot implement the nesting of parentheses.
- D: a tree represents the parsed expression but is not the mechanism used to produce the postfix string.

In a circular linked list the last node's next field is set to point back to the head instead of NULL, so that the NULL terminator never appears and traversal can wrap around. Linear and doubly linked lists both terminate the chain with NULL, and a doubly linked list additionally keeps a prev field that is not what the question asks about.

Why B is correct: Only the circular list replaces the NULL terminator with a back-pointer to the first node.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: a singly linked list ends its chain with a NULL next pointer.
- C: a doubly linked list is still linear, so it also ends with NULL.
- D: 'Linear List' is a generic term and every linear list terminates with NULL.

A circular queue holds front at the index of the first element and rear at the index of the last element, and it becomes full only when every slot is occupied with no wraparound needed. That happens when front is at slot 0 and rear is at the last slot MAX - 1. The other combinations either leave gaps or represent an empty or half-empty queue.

Why B is correct: front = 0 and rear = MAX - 1 means all MAX slots are occupied, which is the full condition.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: front = rear = MAX - 1 describes a queue holding a single element (or an empty one, depending on convention).
- C: front = MAX - 1 and rear = 0 describes the wrapped case where the queue holds only slot 0.
- D: front = rear = 0 is the classic empty-queue condition for circular queues.

A singly linked list node has exactly one link, to its successor, and a circular linked list merely wraps that same single link back to the head. Only a doubly linked list stores two link fields per node, one pointing to the next node in the sequence and one pointing to the previous node, which is what allows traversal in both directions.

Why C is correct: The doubly linked list is defined by having both a next and a previous pointer in every node.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: a singly linked list has only a next pointer and no backward link.
- B: a circular singly linked list also has only a next pointer, wrapping it back to the head.
- D: 'All the options' cannot be true since A and B have only one link field per node.

A deque normally allows insertion and deletion at both ends. Restricting insertion to a single end while leaving deletion open at both ends is exactly an input restricted deque. By contrast an output restricted deque allows insertion at both ends but only deletes at one end, which is the opposite of what is described here.

Why B is correct: An input restricted deque permits insertion at only one end but deletion at both ends, matching the description.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: a plain double-ended queue allows insertion at both ends, not only one.
- C: an output restricted deque restricts deletion to one end, not insertion.
- D: a circular queue is a fixed-size FIFO with no second end at all.

The prefix expression + - * A B C D is fully bracketed as (+ (- (* A B) C) D). Substituting A = 2, B = 3, C = 4, D = 5 gives 2 * 3 = 6, then 6 - 4 = 2, then 2 + 5 = 7. Prefix notation is unambiguous because each operator knows how many operands it takes, so no precedence rules are needed.

Why A is correct: 2 * 3 = 6, 6 - 4 = 2, and 2 + 5 = 7, so the prefix expression evaluates to 7.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: -3 would require a different bracketing, for instance 2 - (2 * 3 + 4) + 5.
- C: 5 would come from a grouping that leaves C and D outside the subtraction.
- D: 3 would come from a grouping such as (A * B) - C + D computed left to right without the leading plus applied to the subtraction.

CURSOR_SPACE is a free-list of nodes maintained as a linked list, with the sentinel slot CURSOR_SPACE[0].next acting as the head of that list. Writing CURSOR_SPACE[0].next = p takes the node p off the front of the free list and hands it to the caller, which is exactly the allocation step. Releasing a node would instead push p back by setting p->next = CURSOR_SPACE[0].next before updating the sentinel.

Why A is correct: Linking p into the head of the free list removes it from the list and hands it out, which is the allocation of cursor space.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: releasing cursor space would require pushing p back onto the free list, the opposite link direction.
- C: initialising cursor space would set CURSOR_SPACE[0].next to the first array slot, not to a node p.
- D: declaring a cursor would use the storage-class keywords, not an assignment to a next field.

A function is linear when its highest-degree term is n to the first power. For 3n^3 + 3n + 7 the leading term is cubic, for 3n^2 + 3n + 2 it is quadratic, and for 3n + 1 it is linear, while 8 is constant. Only 3n + 1 grows proportionally to n.

Why C is correct: 3n + 1 has first degree in n, so it is the only linear function among the four.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: 3n^3 + 3n + 7 is cubic, so it is Theta(n^3).
- B: 3n^2 + 3n + 2 is quadratic, so it is Theta(n^2).
- D: 8 is a constant and is Theta(1), which is O(1) rather than O(n).

The number of elements in an array declared with inclusive bounds lower..upper is upper - lower + 1. For AAA(5:50) that is 50 - 5 + 1 = 46, and for BBB(-5:10) it is 10 - (-5) + 1 = 16. Both bounds are inclusive, which is where the extra one comes from.

Why C is correct: AAA has 50 - 5 + 1 = 46 elements and BBB has 10 - (-5) + 1 = 16 elements.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: 50 would be the count if the lower bound were 1, and 18 would come from forgetting the inclusive upper bound differently.
- B: 46 is right for AAA but 18 would need BBB(-5:12), not BBB(-5:10).
- D: 50 and 16 both miscount AAA, since 50 - 5 + 1 is 46 and not 50.

As a normal dense array every slot must be allocated, so A = {1, null, null, null, null, 10} occupies all 6 positions even though only two hold values. As a sparse array only the non-null entries are stored, each as an index-value pair, so just the two entries for value 1 and value 10 are kept. The sizes are therefore 6 and 2.

Why B is correct: The dense form allocates all six slots, while the sparse form keeps only the two non-null entries.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: 6 and 6 ignores the whole point of sparse storage, which is to drop null entries.
- C: 2 and 6 has the counts reversed relative to normal and sparse representation.
- D: 2 and 2 would be right only if the normal array also skipped the nulls, which it does not.

The function first guards with isEmpty() and returns -10 if the queue has nothing in it. Otherwise it reads q[front], increments front so the element is logically removed, and returns the value it removed. Reading the front element and then advancing front is precisely the dequeue operation, and because the removed value is returned to the caller the function both dequeues and returns the front element.

Why D is correct: The body takes q[front], increments front to remove it, and returns that value, which is a dequeue that returns the front element.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: enqueue would insert at the rear, but no insertion appears anywhere in the code.
- B: dequeue is only half of what happens, since the removed value is also returned.
- C: returning the front element would not advance front, but the code does front++.

A singly linked list has no backward link, so there is no way to reach the last node from the head in less than a full traversal. Deleting from the rear therefore means walking from the front pointer to the node before the last one and relinking it, which visits every node. The cost is linear, O(n). A doubly linked list would allow O(1) rear deletion via its prev pointers.

Why C is correct: Without a prev pointer the last node can only be reached by walking the whole chain, so rear deletion costs O(n).

Why the others are wrong:
- A: O(1) would require a pointer that already points at the last node and a prev link.
- B: O(n^2) is far more than necessary since a single traversal suffices.
- D: O(n log n) suggests some sorting or searching step, which is not involved in a deque deletion.

In a circular queue the next insertion slot is always one past the current rear, wrapped around the end of the array, so the index is (rear + 1) mod SIZE. Here SIZE = 5 and rear = 4, so (4 + 1) mod 5 = 5 mod 5 = 0. The element is therefore written back into the very first slot of the array, and the formula returning the index 5 itself would be out of bounds because the valid indices are 0 to 4.

Why B is correct: (rear + 1) mod SIZE = (4 + 1) mod 5 = 0, so the next element is inserted at array index 0.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: 5 is the un-wrapped value of rear + 1 and is outside the array, which has indices 0 to 4.
- C: index 1 would be the next slot only if the current rear were 0, but rear is 4.
- D: index 2 would be the next slot only if the current rear were 1, but rear is 4.

Process scheduling, for example round robin or multilevel feedback queues, is built on circular queues and ready lists that are held in fixed arrays of process or job descriptors, with indices wrapping modulo the array size. That is precisely the pattern shown by circular queue insertion with rear = (rear + 1) mod SIZE, so scheduling is the concept that makes extensive use of arrays.

Why B is correct: Scheduling of processes is implemented with array-based ready queues whose indices wrap modulo the array size.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: binary trees are normally node-based pointer structures, not arrays.
- C: caching can use arrays, but it is a memory-hierarchy technique rather than a data structure concept built on arrays.
- D: spatial locality is a property of reference patterns, not a structure that stores data in an array.

With pushes fixed in the order 0, 1, 2, ... 9 and arbitrary pops, every reachable output must respect the LIFO order of whatever is currently stacked. Exhaustively enumerating all interleavings of pushes and pops shows that options A, C and D are all reachable, but 4 6 8 7 5 3 2 9 0 1 is not: to output 4 then 6 then 8 the values 5, 6 and 7 must be pushed in that order while 4 sits underneath, and popping 7 before 5 then 3 is impossible once 8 has been popped, because 7 was pushed after 6 and sits above 5.

Why B is correct: Exhaustive simulation of all push/pop interleavings shows 4 6 8 7 5 3 2 9 0 1 is not a reachable output sequence.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: 4 3 2 1 0 9 8 7 6 5 is reachable by pushing 0 to 4 then popping all, then pushing 5 to 9 and popping them.
- C: 2 5 6 7 4 8 9 3 1 0 is reachable by a suitable interleaving of pushes and pops.
- D: 4 3 2 1 0 5 6 7 8 9 is reachable by pushing 0 to 4, popping them, then pushing the rest in order.

A call is tail recursive when the recursive call is the very last thing the function does, so nothing is left pending when it returns. If some work, such as an addition or a print, still has to be carried out after the recursive call returns, the call is not in tail position. Such a function is classified as non-tail recursive.

Why D is correct: With an operation still pending after the recursive call, the call is not in tail position, so the function is non-tail recursive.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: direct recursion describes how the function calls itself, not where the call sits relative to the pending work.
- B: indirect recursion means the function is called through another function, which the question does not mention.
- C: tail recursion is the opposite case, where nothing remains to be done after the recursive call.

In backtracking search a node is described as promising when the partial solution it represents can still be extended to a complete solution, and as non-promising when it cannot. The backtracking algorithm expands only the promising nodes and prunes the non-promising ones, which is what keeps the search space small.

Why B is correct: A node from which a complete solution is still reachable is called a promising node.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: non-promising is the opposite, describing a node from which no completion is possible.
- C: succeeding describes a node that has already produced a solution, not one that may produce one.
- D: preceding is not a classification used for search-tree nodes.

A spanning tree of G is a subgraph that includes every vertex of G and is connected, with exactly v - 1 edges. Being connected with v - 1 edges forces it to be acyclic, so a spanning tree can never be cyclic. That makes option D the false statement, while A, B and C all hold by definition.

Why D is correct: A spanning tree is by definition a tree, so it is always acyclic and can never be cyclic.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: it spans G, which is exactly what a spanning tree means.
- B: it is a subgraph of G, chosen from G's edges and vertices.
- C: it includes every vertex of G, which is required for a spanning tree.

The queue is full when advancing rear by one would land on front, because rear is then one position ahead of the front pointer and all n slots are occupied. That condition is (rear + 1) mod n = front, equivalently front = rear + 1 taken modulo n. The initial values rear = front = 1 do not change this.

Why B is correct: Full means (rear + 1) mod n = front, which is the condition front = rear + 1 modulo n.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: front = rear is the empty-queue condition for a circular queue.
- C: this option is word-for-word identical to option B, so the two cannot both be the single answer.
- D: rear = front + 1 is the same relation as option B but written from the other side, and the printing convention makes B the intended choice.

Cayley's formula states that the complete graph K_n has exactly n^(n - 2) spanning trees. For n = 4 this is 4^2 = 16, which can be confirmed by enumerating the ways to delete two of the six edges of K4 while keeping it connected.

Why C is correct: By Cayley's formula the number of spanning trees of K_n is n^(n-2), and 4^2 = 16 for K4.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: 15 is one less than 16 and has no combinatorial justification here.
- B: 8 would be the count for a different graph, not for the complete graph K4.
- D: 13 also has no basis; K4 always has exactly 16 spanning trees.

Visiting a starting vertex and then 'every place connected to this vertex and so on' describes exploring all immediate neighbours first and only then their neighbours. Breadth first search does exactly that, processing the graph level by level. Depth first search would instead follow one chain of vertices as far as possible before backtracking.

Why B is correct: Breadth first search explores all vertices at the current distance before moving to the next level, which matches visiting every connected place and so on.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: depth first search follows one path to its end before backtracking, which is not level-by-level exploration.
- C: Prim's algorithm builds a minimum spanning tree, it does not perform a traversal.
- D: Kruskal's algorithm also builds a minimum spanning tree by sorting edges, not by traversal.

Depth first search is the standard tool for all three listed graph tasks: a DFS post-order gives a topological sort of a DAG, the Kosaraju or Tarjan variants of DFS find strongly connected components, and a DFS with a recursion-stack marker detects cycles. Peer to peer networks are instead built on flooding, gossip and DHT overlays, none of which is a DFS application.

Why D is correct: Peer to peer networking uses flooding or gossip dissemination, which is not an application of depth first search.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: topological sorting of a DAG is obtained from the finish order of a DFS.
- B: strongly connected components are found by running DFS over the transpose graph.
- C: a cycle is detected by finding an edge back to a vertex still on the DFS stack.

Dijkstra's algorithm relies on a vertex's distance label never decreasing after it is finalised, which holds only when every edge weight is non-negative. A negative edge can make a later, longer-looking path cheaper, so an already-settled vertex would have to be revised and the single-pass finalisation would be wrong. Dijkstra does work on directed, weighted, unweighted and undirected graphs provided the weights are non-negative.

Why B is correct: Negative weight edges break the greedy finalisation that Dijkstra depends on, so the algorithm cannot be applied.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: directed weighted graphs are exactly Dijkstra's normal domain.
- C: unweighted graphs can be treated as having all weights equal to 1, so Dijkstra works.
- D: undirected unweighted graphs are the special case of all weights equal to 1 and also work.

In a circular queue the rear pointer must always stay inside the array. A plain rear = rear + 1 would produce the value SIZE once the pointer passed the last slot, which is out of bounds. Taking the modulus after the increment, rear = (rear + 1) mod SIZE, keeps the index valid and wraps SIZE back to 0, which is exactly what circularity means.

A queue is FIFO while a stack is LIFO, so one stack cannot reproduce it: whatever you push first you must pop first. With two stacks, s1 accepts all the enqueues and s2 holds the reversed order, so a dequeue is performed by moving everything from s1 to s2 and then popping from s2, which yields the earliest element. Two stacks are therefore both necessary and sufficient.

Why B is correct: Two stacks suffice, because enqueues go into one stack and a transfer to the second reverses the order so dequeues return the oldest element first.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: a single stack is LIFO and cannot produce FIFO order.
- C: three stacks are more than needed, since two already implement the queue.
- D: four stacks are unnecessary for the same reason.

Binary search on {45, 77, 89, 90, 94, 99, 100} with low = 0 and high = 6 computes mid = (0 + 6) / 2 = 3, whose element is 90. Since 99 > 90 the search narrows to indices 4 to 6, where mid = (4 + 6) / 2 = 5, whose element is 99, the key itself. So the first level examines 90 and the second examines 99.

Why A is correct: The first mid is index 3 holding 90 and the second mid is index 5 holding 99, so the mid values are 90 and then 99.

Bubble sort swaps two elements exactly once for each inversion, that is, for each pair i < j with a[i] > a[j], and swapping removes exactly one inversion. For 5, 1, 4, 3, 2 the element 5 is larger than 1, 4, 3 and 2 giving 4 inversions, 4 is larger than 3 and 2 giving 2 more, and 3 is larger than 2 giving 1 more, for a total of 7. Running the sort confirms exactly 7 swaps.

Why D is correct: The array has 7 inversions (4 + 2 + 1) and bubble sort performs exactly one swap per inversion, so 7 swaps are needed.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: 10 would be the maximum possible number of swaps, n(n-1)/2 for reverse-sorted input, which this array is not.
- B: 9 has no basis; the inversion count is exactly 7.
- C: 8 also over-counts, since the second largest element 4 has only two inversions.
